task.goal: Make important paper documents retrievable within five minutes in a crowded shared home without exposing private papers to other residents.
hard_constraints: No scanning service or new lockable cabinet; each adult controls their own documents.
A common label system must not reveal document contents.
Test retrieval time, misfiling and upkeep after four weeks.
task.available_resources: Folders, envelopes and one shared shelf.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Opaque packets with a private location index
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: Give every document packet a stable, meaningless address and let its owner maintain a private index linking document names to those addresses. Retrieval becomes a lookup followed by one shelf search, rather than a search through papers.

Each adult chooses a neutral owner code and numbers their folders and opaque envelopes, such as Q7-03-08. The common label format identifies only owner, folder and envelope; it never includes names, institutions, document types or importance. Keep folders in fixed shelf order. Each adult creates and controls their own handwritten index, stored inside an opaque personal envelope. For example, their private entry might connect a passport renewal letter to Q7-03-08. Related papers can share an envelope if the packet remains small enough to inspect quickly. Return borrowed papers to their recorded addresses; index new papers when filing them.

This could work because the index separates semantic information from visible storage labels. It requires enough opaque envelopes, ordinary writing materials, sufficient shelf space and owners willing to update their indexes. It also assumes adults can identify what they need by a name or keyword used in their index. Missing synonyms and stale entries are likely failure points.

Opaque envelopes prevent casual viewing, but cannot prevent a resident deliberately opening them. Without a lock, this system therefore depends on an agreement that residents handle only their own packets. If protection against deliberate access is required, the supplied resources are insufficient.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before setup, have each owner retrieve three privately selected papers from their current arrangement; record times and failures without recording contents publicly. After four weeks, repeat with six varied requests, including recently added papers. Count any retrieval exceeding five minutes. Each owner privately audits ten papers against the index and counts wrong locations and missing entries. Record weekly filing and return minutes. Treat slower retrieval, persistent misfiling or upkeep that owners repeatedly skip as evidence against the system; the small sample cannot establish reliability for every document.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A private branching filing guide
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: Use a short, owner-defined decision tree to narrow each retrieval to a small packet, avoiding a separate index entry for every document. The outcome depends on owners applying the same classification rule when filing and retrieving.

Each adult privately defines a shallow tree based on how they naturally look for papers. For example, its first question might distinguish papers concerning a person from papers concerning a household item; later questions narrow the destination. These meanings appear only on a private handwritten guide inside an opaque envelope. On the shared shelf, folders and envelopes show only a neutral owner code and numbered branch addresses, such as R4-2-1. Everyone follows that content-free label format, but each adult controls their own classification and papers.

Keep the tree shallow and its final packets small. Write a tie-breaking rule for ambiguous papers and a private cross-reference where necessary. A new paper follows the same questions as a retrieval request. If a packet becomes too large to search promptly, its owner divides it and updates the guide. No other resident needs to learn its meanings.

This could reduce upkeep because the guide describes groups rather than tracking every sheet. It requires categories that remain memorable and sufficiently unambiguous, enough opaque envelopes, and shelf capacity for separate adult collections. Its main limits are inconsistent classification and oversized packets. Privacy depends on opaque storage and residents respecting ownership; numeric labels do not prevent deliberate opening.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the owner's existing arrangement as the simple comparator, timing three representative retrievals before changing it. During four weeks, note filing and maintenance minutes privately. At week four, time six retrievals, including one ambiguous and one newly filed document; each should finish within five minutes. Audit ten randomly selected papers for agreement with the written branching rules. Also have the owner classify five document descriptions twice, several days apart, without moving papers. Different destinations reveal ambiguity even if current retrieval happens to succeed. Revise or reject the approach if ambiguity, packet size or upkeep prevents dependable retrieval.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Chronological packets with a private event log
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: Preserve arrival order and use a private chronological log to locate papers by the event that produced them. This replaces topical classification with an append-only record, making filing a predictable sequence.

Each adult reserves opaque envelopes in numbered order within their own folders. Shared labels contain only a neutral owner code and sequence number, such as M8-014; visible labels omit dates and contents. Papers from one event stay together, and each envelope holds only a small, inspectable batch. The owner writes a private log entry giving the date, event description, useful search words and envelope number. Keep the log inside an opaque personal envelope. Existing papers can be logged as initial batches without reconstructing their full history.

When a paper arrives, the owner adds it to the current small batch and records the event. Retrieval starts with the log, then goes directly to the numbered envelope. Removed papers return to that envelope. If a paper moves permanently, amend its log entry. A private list of frequently requested papers can point to their original entries without changing their locations.

This could work well when people remember a transaction, appointment or approximate period more readily than a filing category. Sequential storage avoids repeated category decisions. It requires a legible, manageable log, ordinary writing materials, enough opaque envelopes and regular logging. A long handwritten log or vague event descriptions could defeat the five-minute goal; success is uncertain for large backlogs. As with the other approaches, opaque storage protects against casual viewing, while deliberate access requires protections unavailable here.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Time three retrievals using the current arrangement before setup. For four weeks, record logging and refiling minutes. At week four, ask each owner to retrieve six papers using mixed cues: an event, an approximate date and a document name. Record elapsed time and failures against five minutes. Privately audit ten papers for correct envelope location and a usable log entry. Include older papers to expose slow log searching. Compare retrieval and upkeep with baseline; frequent missing entries or searches exceeding five minutes would falsify suitability for that household.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A bounded flip-through file with concealed recognition labels
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: Make the entire important-document collection small enough to inspect within five minutes. Retrieval uses direct recognition while flipping through concealed document labels, without maintaining a separate location index or classification guide. The outcome depends on enforcing a measured capacity limit.

Each adult keeps their own closed folders on the shared shelf. All visible labels follow one content-free format: a neutral owner code and folder number. Inside, each document or short related packet sits in an opaque envelope. Its owner writes a descriptive recognition label beneath the envelope flap, readable only when deliberately lifted. Keep the actual papers enclosed while checking labels. No content descriptions appear on exposed surfaces.

The owner searches envelopes in sequence until recognizing the requested packet. Envelopes need no topical or chronological order, and a returned packet can occupy any position within that owner's collection. New papers require only an envelope and concealed label. This removes location-update errors, although papers can still enter the wrong adult's folder or receive unclear labels.

At setup, each owner identifies the papers covered by the five-minute promise and measures a complete flip-through, including opening folders and extracting a packet. Keep sufficient margin below five minutes. Other papers remain separately enclosed in that adult's folders, clearly distinguished only through private internal markings. If all important papers cannot fit within the measured search capacity, this approach is unsuitable; adding folders does not solve that limit.

Implementation needs folders that conceal their contents, opaque envelopes, a pen, sufficient shelf space and a timer. Each adult chooses and handles their own papers. Privacy assumes residents respect closed personal storage: these resources can prevent casual viewing but cannot prevent deliberate opening. Label ambiguity, growing collections and crowded access remain uncertainties.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before setup, time three privately chosen retrievals from each adult's current arrangement. Run the proposed system for four weeks and record weekly filing and return minutes. At week four, time six retrievals, including a newly added paper and one near the end of the sequence, plus one complete inspection. Count requests exceeding five minutes. Privately inspect every envelope for wrong-owner papers, misleading labels and loose or misplaced contents; report counts without document names. Reject the approach if the full collection exceeds the time budget, any requested paper cannot be located, or upkeep is repeatedly skipped. Compare retrieval failures and weekly effort with the original arrangement; a small successful trial supports local feasibility, not guaranteed reliability.

EXPAND.title: Owner-arranged spatial memory folders
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: Use remembered physical positions to locate documents, rather than translating document names through an index, classification tree or chronological log. Each adult creates a stable arrangement of opaque envelopes inside their own folders and rehearses finding important papers there.

Use a common external label format containing only an arbitrary owner code and folder number. Inside each folder, keep envelopes in a fixed sequence. Each owner chooses positions directly: a frequently needed paper might occupy the first envelope in the second folder, for example. Position assignments need not follow categories. Keep unrelated documents in separate envelopes where supplies permit; keep inseparable document sets together. Never insert an envelope between existing positions: append new ones or deliberately rearrange and rehearse the affected folder. Return papers immediately to their original envelopes.

The working principle is learned location memory. Repeated retrieval can make a paper’s physical position familiar without maintaining a written lookup entry. Each adult controls their arrangement; other residents only need to respect the externally identified ownership boundaries. Folders stay together on the shared shelf, but their shelf position can change without changing the internal arrangement.

This requires opaque envelopes, enough folders, ordinary marking materials and a collection small enough for its owner to learn. It is most plausible for a limited set of important papers, not hundreds of rarely used items. Memory decay, similar envelopes and interruptions during refiling are material weaknesses. Adults must personally judge which papers belong in their important collection; this method does not locate papers excluded from it.

Closed envelopes conceal contents during ordinary shelf use. Retrieval should occur away from other residents. These resources cannot prevent someone deliberately opening another person’s envelopes; the household must accept an explicit ownership agreement for privacy against casual exposure.
EXPAND.experiment: Before setup, time three retrievals using the owner’s current arrangement. After four weeks of ordinary use, privately select six important papers, including two not retrieved during that month, and time retrieval from the initial request through finding the actual paper. Any result above five minutes challenges the approach. Privately inspect ten envelopes for papers returned to the wrong position, and total weekly filing, rehearsal and rearrangement minutes. Compare with baseline. If success depends on repeated practice that the owner skips, or unused locations are forgotten, reject the method for that owner rather than treating rehearsal-day speed as sufficient evidence.

EXPAND.title: A bounded collection searched directly
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: Make a complete direct search short enough to meet the target. Instead of predicting where a document belongs, each adult maintains a compact collection of important papers that can be inspected from beginning to end within five minutes.

Each adult places their important documents in opaque envelopes within personally controlled folders. Use the same content-free external label convention for everyone: arbitrary owner code and consecutive container numbers. Numbers distinguish containers; they do not encode document types or point to a separate index. Within the collection, no classification is required. On retrieval, the owner takes their folders to a private surface and inspects envelopes in a consistent sequence until the document is found. Return it to its envelope afterward.

What changes the outcome is a verified upper bound on the amount of material searched. During setup, each adult rehearses a complete inspection, including fetching folders and opening envelopes. Reduce bulky packaging or separate irrelevant enclosures where appropriate, without discarding necessary records. If the complete collection cannot be inspected comfortably within five minutes, this alternative is unsuitable for that adult. Do not obtain a passing result by excluding papers the adult considers important.

New important papers can be appended without a classification decision or log entry. Every addition consumes part of the search-time allowance, so the owner repeats the complete inspection when the collection grows appreciably. This trades slower average retrieval for minimal filing complexity and an observable worst-case search route.

It requires a sufficiently small important-document collection, adequate envelopes and shelf space, and private room to inspect contents. It may work especially well where failed filing habits cause more trouble than collection size. Capacity is uncertain until measured. Opaque envelopes prevent casual viewing, but residents must agree not to open one another’s papers; the supplied resources cannot enforce that boundary.
EXPAND.experiment: Time three representative retrievals from the existing arrangement as a comparator. At week four, time a complete inspection and six actual retrievals, including the document encountered last in the search sequence and a recent addition. Each retrieval must finish within five minutes. Privately audit ten papers for placement outside the owner’s collection, mixing between owners or incomplete document sets; topical placement is deliberately irrelevant. Record weekly filing and capacity-check minutes. Reject the approach if growth breaks the time bound, necessary papers are omitted to preserve speed, or upkeep exceeds what the owner consistently performs. A single successful inspection establishes current feasibility, not future capacity.
